extracted.intended_audience: taxonomists, naturalists, museum curators, and freshwater invertebrate biologists (early-20th-century field and museum workers)
extracted.subtask_description: Diagnostic criteria for identifying genera/species of freshwater Plumatellidae and related freshwater sponges, plus practical laboratory methods for preserving and preparing specimens (spicules, gemmules, statoblasts, Hydra, polyzoa) for microscopic examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus diagnosis: Stolella
rubrics_metrics.description: The zoarium consists of groups of zooecia (or occasionally of single zooecia) joined together by an adherent rhizome. There is no gelatinous investment. The adult zooecia resemble those of Plumatella except in being sometimes more or less upright. The polypide and statoblasts resemble those of Plumatella. Fixed as well as free statoblasts occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This genus is closely allied to Plumatella and is probably derived from it; the root-like tube arises from elongation of the basal part of a zooecium and zoaria resemble those of P. punctata until several zooecia are produced when the characteristic mode of growth appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species diagnosis: Stolella indica
rubrics_metrics.description: Zoarium adherent and linear, having neither lateral nor vertical branches. Zooecia short and slender, erect or nearly so, distinctly emarginate and furrowed. Ectocyst soft, colourless and transparent but minutely roughened on the surface. Polypide: tentacles number from 30 to 35, rather short and stout, sometimes slightly expanded at tips; stomach comparatively short and abruptly truncated posteriorly. Statoblasts: both free and fixed; variable in form; fixed statoblasts vary from circular to broadly oval; free statoblasts resemble those of Plumatella punctata but sometimes more elongate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TYPE in the Indian Museum. Geographical distribution confined to the Indo-Gangetic Plain. Biology notes: usually fixed to roots of duckweed or stems of plants; tolerates slight brackish water; short-lived in aquaria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subfamily diagnosis: Lophopinæ
rubrics_metrics.description: Zoaria never dendritic but form gelatinous masses which (except in Australella) are cushion-shaped or sack-like. Statoblasts remarkable for large size. Swim-ring always well developed. Fixed statoblasts are unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With the possible exception of Australella, zoaria possess limited power of movement along surfaces. Australella is intermediate in structure between Plumatellinæ and Lophopinæ and has statoblasts of intermediate size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus diagnosis: Lophopodella
rubrics_metrics.description: Zoarium consists of a circular or oval mass of no great size; polyparia do not form compound colonies. Polypides lie semi-recumbent in the mass and never stand upright. Statoblasts of considerable size, normally bearing at both ends a series of chitinous processes armed with double rows of small curved spinules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The genus is usually recognized by statoblasts, but the processes may be abortive or absent making distinction from Lophopus difficult; Indian species have statoblasts shaped distinctly unlike known Lophopus species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species diagnosis: Lophopodella carteri
rubrics_metrics.description: Zoarium oval when polypides expanded; mound-shaped in side view; polypides radiate from a common centre often in several circles; ectocyst much swollen, hyaline and colourless. Polypide normally about 60 tentacles; velum narrow and not strongly festooned; stomach yellow or greenish. Extended polypide ~3 mm; lophophore limbs about same. Statoblast variable but average ~0.85 × 0.56 mm; ends truncate or subtruncate; capsule small compared with swim-ring; end processes variable in number with spinules in two parallel rows, not very numerous and curving round through most of a circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statoblast measurements and details of processes/spinulation are important for identification. Zoaria occur on lower surfaces of stones and stems/leaves of water-plants; zoaria are able to change position slowly (observed to congregate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Varietal diagnosis: Lophopodella carteri var. himalayana
rubrics_metrics.description: Differs from typical form in having fewer tentacles and in that the marginal processes of the statoblast are abortive or absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The abortive processes appear to represent arrested development, since they are among the last parts of the statoblast to be formed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus diagnosis: Pectinatella
rubrics_metrics.description: Adult zoaria always embedded together in groups in a gelatinous investment (thought to be secreted in common). Statoblasts entirely surrounded by processes that bear curved spinules at their tips only. Polypides semi-recumbent but larger than in Lophopodella or Lophopus. Statoblasts larger than those of any other Plumatellidæ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type species P. magnifica; compound colonies often very large (over 2 metres in some species); common investment sometimes contains green cells (algal) giving a dark greenish colour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species diagnosis: Pectinatella burmanica
rubrics_metrics.description: Zoaria circular or nearly so, ~2 cm diameter; polypides arranged into four fan-like groups dividing the zoarium into two main and then two subordinate divisions at right angles. Number of zoaria in colony variable (from ~6 to several hundreds). Common investment often up to two inches thick and translucent dark greenish due to green cells. Polypide extrudable at least 5 mm; about 90 tentacles long and slender; velum narrow and almost straight. Statoblasts large (1–1.75 mm diameter), almost circular with one side slightly flattened; marginal processes very short bearing a single pair of hooks at the tip; capsule circular and small compared with swim-ring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type in Indian Museum. Biology: larvae are pear-shaped ~2 mm, swim broad-end-first by cilia, settle and fix by nightfall, then evert two polypides; statoblasts may lie dormant in dry seasons and germinate with rains; common investment contains characteristic green algal cells—investigate further.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statoblast morphology for identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Statoblast shape, size, presence/absence/shape of marginal processes, spinule arrangement, capsule size relative to swim-ring, and whether statoblasts are fixed or free are diagnostic characters at genus and species level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples across genera: Lophopodella—processes armed with double rows of small curved spinules; Pectinatella—processes with curved spinules at tips only; some genera have abortive or absent processes making identification harder. Measurements (e.g., 0.85 × 0.56 mm for L. carteri; 1–1.75 mm for P. burmanica) are useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zoarium and colony-form characters as diagnostic criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether zoaria are dendritic or never dendritic; whether they form gelatinous masses, cushion-shaped or sack-like colonies; whether zoaria are adherent and linear, circular masses, compound colonies with common investment, or consist of groups joined by adherent rhizome are key characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare Plumatella (dendritic forms common) versus Lophopinæ (never dendritic). Colony habit, ability to move slowly along surfaces, and presence/absence of a gelatinous investment distinguish genera and subfamilies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species differentiation: Ephydatia fluviatilis vs E. meyeni
rubrics_metrics.description: E. fluviatilis differs from E. meyeni in: (i) absence of bubble-cells in the parenchyma; (ii) less spongin in the skeleton which is less compact; (iii) gemmule-spicules longer, shafts generally longer than the diameter of the rotulæ; (iv) gemmules armed with a single row of regularly arranged spicules embedded in pneumatic tissue with minute air-spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sponge is variable; certain 'varieties' previously described are encompassed by E. fluviatilis. External form often influenced by environment (disk-like films on stones, cockscomb-like on twigs, nodules among water-weeds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Species diagnosis: Corvospongilla caunteri (new species)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sponge forming thin films not more than 3–4 mm thick, bright green, moderately hard but friable; surface smooth; oscula inconspicuous with shallow radiating furrows; stout basal membrane. Skeleton reticulate but almost devoid of spongin; reticulations close formed mainly by single spicules; close layer of spicules parallel to basal membrane. Skeleton-spicules variable, almost straight, blunt or abruptly pointed; flesh-spicules minute and few; gemmule-spicules amphistrongylous or amphioxous, irregularly spiny. Gemmules free in the substance, spherical or depressed, variable in size but never large, with a thick external pneumatic coat (air-spaces extremely small) and inside it a single sparse layer of spicules parallel to the gemmule; single depressed aperture present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TYPE in the Indian Museum. Habitat: Hazratganj, Lucknow on bridge piers in running water. Gemmule structure differs considerably from other known species of Corvospongilla where gemmules are usually adherent and lack a true pneumatic coat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation guideline: Spongillidæ
rubrics_metrics.description: Spongillidæ must be preserved dry or in very strong alcohol. Formalin should not be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid formalin for Spongillidæ preservation; choose dry or strong alcohol methods to maintain specimen integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure: Cleaning siliceous sponge spicules
rubrics_metrics.description: Place small fragments of dried sponge in a test tube, cover with strong nitric acid and boil until solid particles disappear. Add a large quantity of water, filter through pure cellulose filter-paper with agitation, wash filter repeatedly with clean water, dry filter, coil it in wire and ignite so spicules fall into a receptacle. Pick up spicules with a camel's-hair brush and mount in Canada balsam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If alcohol is present with the dried sponge, the reaction may be violent — ensure dryness. Use care when igniting filter-paper to collect spicules; mount in Canada balsam for microscopy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure: Examining the skeleton of a Spongillid
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut thin hand-sections with a sharp scalpel, dehydrate if necessary, and mount in Canada balsam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thin hand-sections reveal skeletal structure; dehydrate (through alcohols) before mounting if required for clarity and preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure: Preparing gemmules for examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Place gemmules dry in a watch-glass with a few drops of strong nitric acid. When gas is given off freely add water in considerable quantities. Remove gemmules with a camel's-hair brush to clean water, then to 50%, 70%, 90% and absolute alcohol in succession, leaving them for an hour in each strength. Clear with oil of cloves and mount in Canada balsam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gradual dehydration through alcohol series recommended; clearing with oil of cloves before mounting in Canada balsam yields good optical results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure: Ascertaining presence of bubble-cells in parenchyma
rubrics_metrics.description: Tease up a small piece of the sponge with a pair of needles, mount under a thin cover-slip in strong spirit, and examine under a high power of the microscope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strong spirit as mounting medium for teasing and high-power microscopy to reveal bubble-cells; prepare small delicate mounts to avoid crushing structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure: Preserving Hydra in an expanded condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the polyp in a watch-glass of clean water until its tentacles are expanded. Heat a few drops of commercial formaldehyde and squirt the liquid while still hot at the Hydra, which will be killed instantaneously. Remove it to a solution of commercial formaldehyde and spirit of formula: commercial formaldehyde 1 part; absolute alcohol 3 parts; distilled water 7 parts. Then pass the Hydra through 50% and 70% alcohol and keep in 90%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Killing with hot formaldehyde fixes the expanded form. Follow with graded alcohol for storage; this method preserves tentacle expansion for anatomical study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure: Examining capsules of nettle-cells (cnidocysts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a living Hydra in a small drop of water on a slide and press a thin cover-slip down upon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple squash preparation from living material allows observation of nematocyst capsules under the microscope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure: Preserving freshwater polyzoa in an expanded condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the polyzoa in a glass tube full of clean water and allow them to expand their tentacles. Drop on them gradually when fully expanded a 2% aqueous solution of cocaine, two or three drops at a time, until movement ceases in the tentacles. Then pour commercial formaldehyde into the tube in considerable quantities. Allow to stand for half an hour. If staining for anatomy is desired, then remove through 50% and 70% to 90% alcohol. If desired to keep life-like, keep permanently in a solution of one part commercial formaldehyde in four parts water. Preserve duplicate specimens in spirit or formalin with the lophophore retracted. Care must be taken that paralyzing is not unduly prolonged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cocaine used as a paralytic; do not prolong paralysis; preserve duplicates in different states (expanded and retracted) depending on future needs (anatomy vs life-like appearance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure: Preparing statoblasts for examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Place statoblasts for a few minutes in strong nitric acid. Remove the acid with water, pass through alcohol, clear with oil of cloves, and mount in a small quantity of Canada balsam under a cover-slip, taking care that the statoblasts lie parallel to the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use brief nitric-acid treatment to clean statoblasts, then graded alcohol dehydration, clearing and mounting with careful orientation (parallel to cover-slip) for optimal microscopic observation.
